prompt: What does the final `.1` in `go1.27.1` say?
hint: Section 04 names the two numbers.

choices.text: It is a beta, before the stable go1.27.2
choices.why: Go names its pre-releases `rc` or `beta`; a three-number name is a release.

choices.text: It is the first fix release of Go 1.27
choices.why: Right. 27 is the major release, and 1 the minor revision that fixes it.

choices.text: It is a new language version, with syntax 1.27.0 lacked
choices.why: The language version is 1.27 for every 1.27.x; fix releases change no syntax.

choices.text: It is the build of 1.27 made for Linux on amd64
choices.why: The system is separate: `go version` printed `linux/amd64` after the release name.

prompt: Put these changes in the order the releases that brought them came out, earliest first.
hint: Go 1 first, the loop variable last.

prompt: Match each release with what it brought.
hint: Section 02 dates each one.

pairs.right: The compiler and runtime written in Go
Downloading another Go when a module asks for one

prompt: Lesson 1 built the go command from its source with nothing but Go installed. What made that possible?
hint: Read the two lines of `src/cmd/dist/README` again.

choices.text: The source ships precompiled, so nothing was really compiled
choices.why: The empty cache made it compile 334 packages; the 21 seconds were real work.

choices.text: The lab's `gcc` compiled the parts written in C
choices.why: Since 1.5 there are no such parts: compiler and runtime are Go, with a little assembler.

choices.text: Since Go 1.5 the compiler toolchain is itself written in Go
choices.why: Right. Go compiles Go, so a Go installation is all it takes.

choices.text: The go command downloads a C compiler from the proxy
choices.why: The proxy serves Go toolchains and modules; no C compiler came from it.

prompt: A file that starts with `//go:build go1.21` is compiled only by Go 1.21 and ___ releases.
hint: Each release tag holds from that release onward.

prompt: With `go 1.21` in `go.mod`, what did the loop program print?
hint: One `i` for the whole loop.

choices.why: That was `go 1.22`, where each turn has its own `i`.
Right. All three functions shared one `i`, which had reached 3.
The loop stops when `i` becomes 3, and that last value is what the shared variable holds.
The loop made three functions, for 0, 1 and 2; there is no fourth.

prompt: Between `[3 3 3]` and `[0 1 2]`, what changed?
hint: Same file, same compiler.

choices.text: The toolchain, from go1.21 to go1.22
choices.why: go1.27.1 compiled both runs; `GOTOOLCHAIN` was `local`.

choices.text: Only the `go` line of `go.mod`
choices.why: Right. `go mod edit -go=1.22` was the whole difference, and the compiler kept each version's meaning.

choices.text: The loop in `main.go`, edited between the runs
choices.why: The file was put once and never touched again.

choices.text: A `GODEBUG` setting that `go list` switched off
choices.why: Loop variables are the language and follow the `go` line directly; `GODEBUG` covers the library.

prompt: go1.27.1 refused the generic `Biggest` while `go.mod` said `go 1.17`. Why?
hint: `-lang was set to go1.17`.

choices.text: Generics need `GOTOOLCHAIN=auto` to be switched on
choices.why: `GOTOOLCHAIN` chooses a release, not a feature; with `go 1.18` it compiled under `local`.

choices.text: go1.27.1 dropped the 2022 form of generics
choices.why: The same code ran as soon as the line said `go 1.18`, so nothing was dropped.

choices.text: A feature newer than the `go` line is a compile error
choices.why: Right, even when the compiler has it: the module claimed to need only 1.17.

choices.text: The module had to be downloaded from the proxy first
choices.why: It was a local module; nothing was missing except permission from its own `go` line.

prompt: Which of these are part of the Go 1 compatibility promise, as section 03 quotes it? Choose all that apply.
hint: It is about source code.

choices.text: Source written for Go 1 keeps compiling and running correctly
choices.why: Yes, over the lifetime of the Go 1 specification.

choices.text: A compiled package from one release works with the next
choices.why: The document excludes that: compatibility is at the source level, and binaries are rebuilt.

choices.text: A new toolchain changes the meaning of old modules to the newest rules
choices.why: The opposite: a module that says `go 1.21` kept `[3 3 3]` under go1.27.1.

choices.text: Upgrading the toolchain does not oblige you to edit your code
choices.why: Yes. Code changes meaning only when somebody moves its `go` line.

prompt: A module that says `go 1.21` has `httpmuxgo121=1` among its default `GODEBUG` settings. What does that setting do?
hint: The table said `Package: "net/http"`.

choices.text: It forces the go1.21 toolchain to be downloaded
choices.why: Toolchains are `GOTOOLCHAIN`'s business; `GODEBUG` changes behaviour inside the one that runs.

choices.text: It keeps `net/http`'s `ServeMux` behaving as in Go 1.21
choices.why: Right. The default changed in 1.22, and `Old: "1"` restores what came before.

choices.text: It turns on debug logging for every HTTP request
choices.why: Despite the name, these settings select old or new behaviour; none of them is a logger.

choices.text: It makes the server speak a protocol called HTTP 1.21
choices.why: The 121 is Go 1.21, the release whose router it keeps.

prompt: A teammate's pull request moves a module's `go` line from `go 1.21` to `go 1.24`, "just to be current". Going by section 03, what deserves a reviewer's attention?
hint: What did the edit change in the loop program?

choices.text: Nothing: the `go` line is documentation the compiler reads past
choices.why: The loop program printed two different results on that line alone.

choices.text: Code whose meaning moves with the line, like loops and `GODEBUG` defaults
choices.why: Right. Crossing 1.22 changes every loop variable, and the held-back `GODEBUG` settings go back to the new defaults.

choices.text: That the build server runs exactly go1.24.0, no newer
choices.why: The line is a minimum; go1.27.1 built every module in this lesson.

choices.text: That the loop now prints `[3 3 3]` instead of `[0 1 2]`
choices.why: It is the other way round: `[3 3 3]` belongs to `go 1.21`.

prompt: In which months did go1.21.0 to go1.27.0 come out?
hint: Read the `Time` fields.

choices.text: Whenever each was ready
choices.why: Seven releases in seven alternating Februaries and Augusts is a calendar, not readiness.

choices.text: January and July
choices.why: None of the `Time` fields falls in either month.

choices.text: February and August
choices.why: Right, one each, every year.

choices.text: March and September, like go1 and go1.5
choices.why: go1 came out in March and go1.5 in August; the calendar of recent releases is February and August.

prompt: With go1.27 the newest release, which releases receive fix releases?
hint: `SECURITY.md` says how many.

choices.text: Only go1.27, the newest
choices.why: go1.26.8 came out together with go1.27.1, so 1.26 is fixed too.

choices.text: go1.26 and go1.27
choices.why: Right: the past two releases. 1.25 stopped when 1.27 arrived.

choices.text: go1.25, go1.26 and go1.27, the last three
choices.why: go1.25.14 came out with go1.27.0, and then no go1.25.15 ever did.

choices.text: Every release since go1.21, the first with toolchain modules
choices.why: Being downloadable from the proxy is not being supported; the proxy answered `not found` for go1.25.15.

prompt: On 18 August 2026 go1.27.0 was recorded at 21:24:23 and go1.25.14 and go1.26.7 at 21:44:21. How many minutes later were the fix releases recorded? Give a whole number.
hint: Subtract and round.

prompt: The second `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.0 go version` printed no `downloading` line. Why?
hint: Where does a downloaded toolchain go?

choices.text: The first run replaced `/usr/local/go` with go1.26.0
choices.why: The lab's own Go was untouched; plain `go run .` still printed go1.27.1 afterwards.

choices.text: The lab blocks the network after one download
choices.why: The proxy answered later in the same lesson, when go1.25.0 was downloaded.

choices.text: The toolchain was already in the module cache under `~/go`
choices.why: Right. A toolchain is a module, and it is cached like one.

choices.text: Without a `go.mod` asking for it, `go version` reads the version from memory
choices.why: `go version` ran the toolchain it named; it printed go1.26.0 because that release ran.

prompt: Your laptop has go1.26.3 and the default `GOTOOLCHAIN`. You clone a module whose `go.mod` says `go 1.27.1` and run `go build`. What happens?
hint: What does `go.env` set, and what did `go1.24.0+auto` do?

choices.text: The go command downloads go1.27.1 and builds with it
choices.why: Right. The default is `auto`, and a newer `go` line is fetched rather than refused.

choices.text: It stops: `go.mod requires go >= 1.27.1`
choices.why: That is `GOTOOLCHAIN=local`, the lab's choice, not the default a release ships with.

choices.text: It builds with go1.26.3, since 1.26 is still supported
choices.why: Support is about fixes; the `go` line is a minimum, and 1.26.3 is below it.

choices.text: It asks you to lower the `go` line to 1.26
choices.why: The go command never edits that line for you, and lowering it can change what the code means.

prompt: `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.24.0+___` makes the go command begin with 1.24.0 and still switch when a module asks for a newer release.
hint: The same word as the default in `go.env`.

prompt: `go.mod` says `go 1.22` and `toolchain go1.26.0`. Under `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.24.0+auto`, which release compiled the program?
hint: Which line asks for more than 1.24.0?

choices.text: go1.24.0, which already satisfies `go 1.22`
choices.why: It satisfies the minimum, but the `toolchain` line prefers a newer release and `auto` honours it.

choices.text: go1.26.0, the one the `toolchain` line names
choices.why: Right: it printed `compiled by go1.26.0`.

choices.text: go1.22.0, the one the `go` line names
choices.why: The `go` line is a minimum, never a request for that exact release.

choices.text: go1.27.1, the newest installed in the lab
choices.why: That happened under `local`; with `+auto` the choice started from 1.24.0.

prompt: A server still runs go1.25.14 in October 2026. Which statements are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Combine the support rule with the proxy's `not found`.

choices.text: It will receive no more fix releases, security ones included
choices.why: Yes. 1.25 stopped when 1.27 arrived; there is no go1.25.15.

choices.text: It is supported, because it is the latest 1.25 release
choices.why: Being the last fix of 1.25 is not being supported; two newer releases exist.

choices.text: Moving to go1.27.1 should not require editing source that builds with 1.25
choices.why: Yes. That is the Go 1 promise; the module's `go` line keeps old meanings until somebody moves it.

choices.text: Upgrading means every module's `go` line must move to 1.27
choices.why: go1.27.1 built modules that said `go 1.21`; the line is a minimum.

prompt: The proxy answered `not found` for the fix release go1.25.___, because 1.25 was no longer supported.
hint: One after the last fix that did come out.
